verbatim: Phares S, Phillip K, Trusheim M. Clinical development success rates for durable cell and gene therapies. Nature Reviews Drug Discovery 24(5):329-330 (2025). Published online 27 February 2025; print issue May 2025. DOI 10.1038/d41573-025-00036-8. PMID 40016384. Affiliation (all three authors, per the Nature page): NEWDIGS, Tufts Medical Center, Boston, MA, USA. Article type: Biobusiness Brief (PubMed publication type 'News'). ISSN 1474-1776 / 1474-1784. Publisher Springer Nature. Supplementary information PDF: https://media.nature.com/original/magazine-assets/d41573-025-00036-8/50677254
notes: Bibliographic fields verified across the Nature article page (title, authors, affiliation, date, DOI), PubMed efetch XML (PMID, volume/issue/pages, dates) and Crossref (online 27 Feb 2025, print May 2025). PubMed record notes Mark Trusheim's competing-interest affiliation with Co-Bio Consulting LLC. NEWDIGS announcement page (25 March 2025) states the research was supported by a grant from the Alliance for Regenerative Medicine. Data source: NEWDIGS FoCUS Pipeline Analysis Model (PAM) built from ClinicalTrials.gov, with trials first identified in Citeline PharmaProjects; comparators are BIO 'Clinical Development Success Rates and Contributing Factors 2011-2020' and IQVIA 'Global Trends in R&D 2024'. dCGT defined as products that use or modify DNA or RNA intended to give a durable effect from a single administration (CBER gene therapy definition plus durable benefit of at least 18 months): (i) gene replacement in vivo and ex vivo with viral vectors; (ii) TCR and CAR-engineered immune cells; (iii) gene editing (ZFN, TALEN, CRISPR-Cas9); (iv) long-acting DNA plasmids. Only two classes are reported numerically: rare disease (orphan) gene therapy and haematological CAR-T/TCR therapy. Only the paywalled two-page main text was not read; search snippets of it also mention a higher-than-average 'strategic' failure rate in 2022 and 2023 (no number seen).

comparator_label: BIO all modalities LOA 2011-2020 (IQVIA all modalities 13.2%, 2010-2022)
verbatim: CGTs for orphan gene therapies (27.6% LoA) are 2 to 3.5 times as likely to be approved when they enter Phase I clinical development as the average drug (BIO 7.9% LoA; IQVIA 13.2% LoA; Figure 2).
notes: NOT S06: predecessor NEWDIGS FoCUS Research Brief 2023F210v056 'Are Cell and Gene Therapy programs a better bet?' No phase durations reported in the brief either.

technology_class: haematological CAR-T/TCR therapy [NEWDIGS 2023 brief, 1988-2020 cut; not S06]
verbatim: CAR-T/TCR therapies for hematological oncology (17.2% LoA) are 3.2 times as likely to be approved when entering Phase I compared to the average oncology drug (5.3% LoA; Figure 1 left panel).
notes: NOT S06: predecessor NEWDIGS FoCUS Research Brief 2023F210v056 'Are Cell and Gene Therapy programs a better bet?' (9 October 2023; PAM trials 1988-end 2020; funded by the FoCUS consortium and the Alliance for Regenerative Medicine). The brief also states CAR-T/TCRs have 2.3 times the LoA of haematological oncology drugs (BIO), and CGTlive reports a 100% Phase 3 progression rate for CAR-T/TCRs versus 48% for oncology drugs in that cut.

technology_class: all drugs in CGT-like therapeutic areas [BIO composite, NEWDIGS 2023 brief; not S06]
comparator_label: orphan gene therapy LoA (rounded) in the 2023 brief
verbatim: CGT orphan gene therapies are still more than twice as likely to be approved as the average drug in similar therapeutic areas (28 % LoA / 13% LoA = 2.2X) and outperform in every phase of the clinical development process (Figure 3).
notes: NOT S06: predecessor NEWDIGS FoCUS Research Brief 2023F210v056 'Are Cell and Gene Therapy programs a better bet?'
